Authors: Mizrak F.; Karakaya T.
Title: Multidimensional Cognitive-State Modeling and an Adaptive Cognitive Load Twin for AI-Supported Managerial Decision-Making
Affiliations: Management Information Systems, Atlas University, Istanbul, 34408, Turkey; Vocational School, Carbon Management Technicianship, Doğuş University, Istanbul, 34680, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Mizrak F., Management Information Systems, Atlas University, Istanbul, 34408, Turkey; Karakaya T., Vocational School, Carbon Management Technicianship, Doğuş University, Istanbul, 34680, Turkey
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported decision systems can improve managerial decision-making, but their cognitive implications may depend on how information, explanations, alerts, time pressure, uncertainty, autonomy, and human control are configured. This study develops an Adaptive Cognitive Load Twin using data from 420 logistics and supply-chain professionals in Türkiye who completed four AI-supported managerial decision scenarios, yielding 1680 participant–scenario observations. The framework models information overload, cognitive load, decision fatigue, perceived explainability, trust in AI, automation bias, perceived human control, perceived decision quality, and objective decision accuracy as distinct but related dimensions. Participant-clustered path analysis showed that higher information overload was associated with higher cognitive load, and higher cognitive load was strongly associated with higher decision fatigue; in turn, higher cognitive load and decision fatigue were associated with lower perceived decision quality. Higher perceived explainability was associated with lower cognitive load, greater trust, higher perceived decision quality, and lower automation-bias tendency, while greater perceived human control was associated with higher perceived decision quality and lower automation bias. Higher cognitive load was associated with lower objective decision accuracy. Participant-grouped machine learning models showed that cognitive load was more predictable than decision fatigue or objective accuracy, with information density and time pressure emerging as leading predictive contributors. Model-based simulations indicated that lower information density and progressive disclosure offered the clearest opportunities for adaptive support. The framework extends digital-twin logic toward multidimensional, human-centered monitoring and adaptation of cognitive conditions in AI-assisted managerial work. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Research Gaps in AI-Supported Disassembly Sequence Planning in Remanufacturing
Affiliations: Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Poznan University of Technology, 1 J. Rychlewski Street, Poznań, 60-965, Poland
Authors with affiliations: Dudkowiak A., Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Poznan University of Technology, 1 J. Rychlewski Street, Poznań, 60-965, Poland; Dostatni E., Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Poznan University of Technology, 1 J. Rychlewski Street, Poznań, 60-965, Poland
Abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly important in research on Disassembly Sequence Planning (DSP). AI-based methods can now solve more complex problems and consider several economic, environmental and operational objectives. However, most studies still focus on optimizing the disassembly process after the recovery strategy and target components have already been selected. This study reviews AI-supported disassembly planning in remanufacturing and identifies the main research gaps and future research directions. The review combines bibliometric mapping of 241 publications with a qualitative analysis of 35 selected studies. Of these studies, 23 directly address DSP, seven concern related disassembly problems, and five focus on remanufacturing planning or scheduling outside DSP. The results show progress in metaheuristic optimization, reinforcement learning, digital twins, knowledge graphs, computer vision, large language models and robotic planning. At the same time, the analysis identified several recurring limitations that can be grouped into three broader dimensions: product-state knowledge and adaptability, validation and transferability, and decision scope and strategic-operational integration. The reviewed studies show that uncertainty, adaptive planning, digital twins and multi-objective optimization have already received considerable attention, but their application remains limited by predefined product representations, case-specific validation and weak integration between product-level recovery assessment and operational disassembly planning. The findings suggest that future research should complement further algorithmic development with more integrated, adaptive and knowledge-supported decision-support approaches that connect recovery assessment with the planning of the required disassembly process. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Integrity of offshore tubular joints: Mechanics, repair strategies, and structural health monitoring towards an integrated lifecycle framework
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Mechanical Engineering, The University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia

Abstract: Offshore tubular joints are critical structural components in fixed and floating offshore platforms, where complex cyclic loading and harsh marine environments can lead to fatigue cracking, corrosion damage, and progressive structural degradation. To extend service life and reduce operational downtime, various repair strategies, including welded reinforcements, grouted systems, and externally bonded fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites, have been widely investigated. However, the long-term performance of repaired tubular joints is strongly influenced by stress redistribution, bondline degradation, environmental exposure, and the effectiveness of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems in detecting early-stage damage. This review critically examines the structural behaviour, failure mechanisms, repair strategies, inspection methods, and SHM technologies associated with repaired offshore tubular joints. Particular emphasis is placed on stress concentration behaviour, fatigue and fracture mechanics, repair-induced load-transfer mechanisms, and interface-controlled degradation in composite-repaired systems. Existing SHM approaches, including fibre optic sensing, acoustic emission, guided waves, and digital monitoring frameworks, are also evaluated in relation to offshore lifecycle integrity management. Furthermore, current standards, qualification procedures, and practical implementation challenges are discussed. Based on the reviewed literature, an integrated mechanics-informed lifecycle framework is proposed to explicitly link damage evolution, measurable SHM features, uncertainty-informed interpretation, and maintenance decision-making. The review identifies key research gaps related to multi-physics modelling, environmental durability, uncertainty quantification, and digital-twin-enabled condition-based maintenance, and highlights future directions toward intelligent and predictive offshore structural integrity management. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Analytic hierarchy process-aware forecasting and economic management in fuel cell-enabled renewable-rich energy clusters with shared hydrogen storage and financial–social welfare considerations
Affiliations: School of Management Engineering and Business, Hebei University of Engineering, Hebei, Handan, 056038, China
Authors with affiliations: Chen Y., School of Management Engineering and Business, Hebei University of Engineering, Hebei, Handan, 056038, China; Kang D., School of Management Engineering and Business, Hebei University of Engineering, Hebei, Handan, 056038, China
Abstract: In this paper, the coordinated welfare-based operation of fuel-cell driven storage-enabled shared mobility for renewable-rich ECCs is considered. To this end, we design a distributed Stackelberg game-theoretic framework with blockchain-enhanced DT management that controls interactions in hierarchy between Shared Hydrogen Transportable (SHT) operator and Energy Communities with access to Shared Electrical Transportable (SET). The welfare-aware hydrogen and electricity exchange prices and dispatch are determined in the upper level, while the lower level obtains each community's optimal operation subject to privacy constraints by using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers. We consider uncertainty using a hybrid approach that incorporates stochastic programming, distributionally robust optimization with Wasserstein ambiguity sets, and Information Gap Decision Theory for low confidence signals. Scenario Generation and Reduction: employs a copula-based joint scenario generator and Kantorovich-Wasserstein planning, and critical security limits are imposed using chance-constrained formulations. A blockchain level is implemented for smart-contract settlements and security, and a DT maintains synchronism of cyber-physical states to underpin adaptive receding-horizon control. Results on tricommunity testbed demonstrate significant cost reduction, higher hydrogen penetration and better peak regulation performance compared to that if each community operates independently while guaranteeing the fairness of benefit distribution under an explicit social welfare constraint. Comparative analysis shows that SHT is superior to SET for multi-hour balancing because of decoupled electrolyzer–fuel-cell scheduling, smaller curtailment, and finer inter-period arbitrage. A refined analytic hierarchy process evaluates composite performance in economic, environmental, and operational dimensions and substantiates cost effectiveness as the most critical priority for ECC. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: Geological CO2 storage, which involves the capture and long-term underground storage of CO2, is a critical technology in mitigating global climate change. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in CO2 storage technologies, focusing on the fundamental mechanisms and engineering implications of multiscale coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical-chemical (THMC) processes. The interactions among thermal, hydrological, mechanical, and chemical processes are further integrated through coupled THMC effects, which are critical for assessing long-term storage integrity and system evolution. Understanding these controlling mechanisms informs the design of both current and emerging engineering applications, highlighting the dual role of CO2 storage while jointly enhancing subsurface resource extraction (such as enhanced coalbed methane (ECBM) and enhanced oil/gas recovery (EOR)) and contributing to decarbonization targets (through dedicated CO2 storage projects). Future perspectives emphasize gigatonne-scale CO2 storage deployment and the integration of CO2 storage with other sustainable technologies, such as CO2-based geothermal energy systems. Key environmental and operational challenges are also addressed, including the risks of leakage, and induced seismicity, together with challenges posed by complex behavior and heterogeneity contributing to reservoir uncertainties, and multi-site co-utilization interactions, all critical for ensuring safe and effective long-term storage. Emerging research directions include multi-scale THMC modeling, measurement-monitoring-verification (MMV) methodologies, and risk assessment empowered by machine learning and digital twins technologies. Deciphering multiscale THMC mechanisms constitutes the foundation for achieving long-term storage security and stability, while simultaneously advancing engineering synergies and climate objectives. © 2026 Institute of Rock and Soil Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences

Title: Coupled biofouling–flow–corrosion prediction and risk assessment of subsea pipelines using bayesian stacked ensembles
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Authors with affiliations: Jagajeevan V., Department of Civil Engineering, Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India; Sivakumar V.L., Department of Civil Engineering, Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Abstract: Subsea pipelines operate in complex environments where hydrodynamic loading, seawater chemistry, and biofouling interact nonlinearly to accelerate material degradation. Accurately predicting erosion–corrosion under such conditions remains challenging, as conventional assessment methods often rely on simplified assumptions that neglect the hydrodynamic regulation of biofilm stability. This study establishes a Coupled Biofouling–Flow–Corrosion modelling framework using a Bayesian Stacked Ensemble approach. Unlike monolithic data-driven models, this framework decomposes degradation into mechanism-specific learners (erosion, electrochemical corrosion, and biofouling-induced amplification) before integrating them to quantify uncertainty. The model is validated using an experimentally-anchored dataset expanded via physics-constrained augmentation, ensuring that predictions remain physically consistent with observed material behavior while covering a wide spectrum of stochastic operating scenarios. The proposed framework demonstrates superior predictive capability (R² ≈ 0.86, MAE < 0.05 mm/yr) and reveals a critical transition from flow-controlled degradation at early exposure to biofouling-dominated corrosion in mature assets. Furthermore, probabilistic risk mapping identifies localized high-uncertainty hotspots that are invisible to deterministic models. These results provide a robust, interpretable tool for Risk-Based Inspection (RBI) planning and Digital Twin integration in offshore energy infrastructure. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors with affiliations: Pan Q., Department of Mechanical and Materials Engineering, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States; Onaga K., Department of Mechanical and Materials Engineering, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States; Li R., Department of Aerospace Engineering and Engineering Mechanics, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States; Dong J., Department of Mechanical and Materials Engineering, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States; Ma O., Department of Aerospace Engineering and Engineering Mechanics, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States; Jia X., Department of Mechanical and Materials Engineering, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, 45221-0072, OH, United States
Abstract: Designing multi-view Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM) systems for multi-robot and multi-human environments remains challenging due to high-dimensional solution space and uncertainties in human behavior. Therefore, this paper presents a novel simulation-driven methodology for multi-view SSM system design that integrates probabilistic modeling of human motion, danger-zone-based safety representation, and voxelized visibility analysis, in multi-robot, multi-human work units. Safety-critical events in the proposed methodology are defined as near-miss human intrusion into dynamically updated robot and end-effector danger zones rather than direct physical contacts. Camera placement optimization is formulated as a joint optimization of positions and orientations to balance coverage, occlusion, and viewpoint diversity. To address the resulting computational complexity, a Parallel Efficient Global Optimization (EGO) approach is adopted to search optimal solution based on computationally expensive digital simulations. The proposed approach is validated in two representative human-robot interaction (HRI) scenarios: a CNC machine tending unit with a single robot and a single human, and palletizing lines with multiple robots and multiple humans. In the CNC machine tending case study, the proposed Parallel EGO method identifies a three-camera layout with no uncovered regions (dark areas) and only 1.25% overall vision occlusions (gray areas). It reduces the number of objective-function evaluations by 74.2% compared with GA and 88.5% compared with NOMAD, while achieving a comparable or lower total loss. In the palletizing case studies, the optimized one-, two-, and three-line layouts requires 3, 6, and 11 cameras, respectively, with dark area percentages of 0%, 0.60%, and 1.43%, and gray area percentages of 6.18%, 14.59%, and 16.36%. © 2026 The Society of Manufacturing Engineers

Title: Beyond the Ranking Paradox: A Context-Weighted Liveability Index for Assessing Mediterranean Smart Cities—A Proof-of-Concept GIS-Based Comparison of Bologna and Athens
Affiliations: Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering (DICEA), University of Padua, Padova, 35131, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Bove A., Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering (DICEA), University of Padua, Padova, 35131, Italy; Ghiraldelli M., Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering (DICEA), University of Padua, Padova, 35131, Italy
Abstract: Conventional international rankings assess urban efficiency via context-blind metrics, a design that the literature suggests may structurally disadvantage Mediterranean centres and obscure the sustainable policy pathways mandated by the Sustainable Development Goals, most notably the governance of urban transitions under SDG 11. This paper proposes the Context-Weighted Liveability Index (CWLI), which introduces context-sensitive weights into the aggregation of standard smart city KPIs, bridging the global comparability of IMD-style indices with the Mediterranean-specific assessment logic of the ASCIMER framework. Weights derive from five geographic coefficients—climate, culture, economy, historical density, and demography—through a transparent weighted additive formulation with an explicit sensitivity matrix, whose robustness is verified through Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis over 5000 perturbed configurations spanning parameters, coefficients, measurements and benchmarks. Coefficients and KPIs are computed from open spatial data through a replicable GIS protocol (QGIS; OpenStreetMap, Copernicus land cover and land surface temperature, and ISTAT/ELSTAT census data at sub-municipal scale). Applied comparatively to Bologna and Athens, the framework shows that contextual weighting concentrates over 60% of the total weight on climate-sensitive indicators and yields, through the decomposition of contributions, a policy diagnosis that differs from the one suggested by reading an overall smart city rank in isolation: Athens’ largest contribution is digital and its liveability deficit territorial—a profile with direct consequences for sustainable urban transition and talent attraction. Implications for SDG 11 monitoring, equitable access to urban green space, and digital twin integration are discussed. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Antiarrhythmic Drug Therapy in Atrial Fibrillation: From Recurrence Prediction to Comparative Treatment Selection

Abstract: Rhythm control therapy has an important role in atrial fibrillation (AF) management, and antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs) remain essential for pharmacological cardioversion, maintenance of sinus rhythm, reduction in AF burden, and treatment before or after catheter ablation. However, their efficacy varies substantially among patients, while proarrhythmia, organ toxicity, drug interactions, and treatment discontinuation frequently limit their use. Current drug selection therefore relies mainly on safety-based exclusion based on structural heart disease, ventricular function, coronary disease, renal or hepatic function, and baseline conduction and repolarization characteristics, rather than on individualized prediction of comparative therapeutic benefit. This narrative review examines the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), computational electrophysiology, and cardiac digital twins across the AAD treatment pathway. Particular attention is given to patient selection, comparative drug choice, prediction of cardioversion success and sinus-rhythm maintenance, dose optimization, proarrhythmia assessment, extracardiac toxicity, and longitudinal safety surveillance. AI can potentially integrate clinical, electrocardiographic (ECG), imaging, wearable, genomic, and pharmacological data to estimate patient-specific efficacy and toxicity. ML models have already demonstrated the feasibility of predicting drug-induced QT prolongation from electronic health records and detecting ECG signatures associated with drug-induced arrhythmic risk. Moreover, patient-specific AF digital twins have been used to simulate electrophysiological responses to amiodarone and identify patients with different subsequent rhythm outcomes. Nevertheless, most available applications remain retrospective, single-center, non-comparative, or proof-of-concept, and few directly support selection among alternative AADs. Most are prognostic, estimate outcomes under observed care, or predict drug-specific toxicity; models that estimate outcomes under alternative AADs remain the essential missing element. AI-supported antiarrhythmic therapy represents a promising transition from population-based prescribing toward individualized estimation of efficacy, toxicity, and monitoring requirements. Its clinical adoption will require multicenter external validation, causal treatment-effect modeling, prospective workflow evaluation, randomized impact trials, transparent uncertainty reporting, and continued clinician oversight. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: A finite-element graph neural network–based method for real-time simulation and evolution analysis of metro bogies

Abstract: Real-time prediction of full-field stress and strain responses is essential for digital twin applications in metro bogie structures. However, existing data-driven approaches face two key challenges: handling extremely high-dimensional finite element outputs with strong spatial correlations, and achieving reliable real-time inference while preserving physical interpretability and uncertainty awareness. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics-informed deep learning framework for fast and reliable full-field stress/strain prediction under operational conditions. The framework integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a finite element–based graph neural network (FEMGNN). The CNN extracts compact latent features from multi-channel vibration signals, while the FEMGNN represents finite element nodes as graph vertices and incorporates element stiffness into edge weights to capture structural topology and physical coupling. By embedding physical and topological information into the learning process, the proposed model enables end-to-end mapping from vibration measurements to node-level stress/strain fields, eliminating the need for independent node-wise modeling and improving both accuracy and computational efficiency. The method can predict full-field responses at more than 18,000 nodes in a single forward pass, with an average inference time of approximately 2.38 ms on a workstation GPU, demonstrating real-time inference potential for digital-twin-based structural monitoring. Furthermore, Monte Carlo Dropout is employed to estimate both predictive means and associated uncertainties, enabling spatial uncertainty visualization and confidence interval analysis. Numerical results under normal operating conditions and multiple crack scenarios demonstrate that the proposed CNN–FEMGNN achieves overall competitive and stable full-field prediction performance compared with CNN-based, CNN–GNN-based, and other surrogate models in terms of accuracy, stability, and uncertainty consistency. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: AI-enabled multi-sensor remote sensing for salt-marsh blue carbon assessment: A scoping review and digital-twin research agenda

Abstract: Salt marshes are climate-relevant blue-carbon ecosystems whose extent, vegetation, hydrology, elevation, biomass and sediment carbon respond to interacting ecological and geomorphic processes. This scoping review synthesizes a frozen inventory of 114 retained records and explicitly separates 23 core empirical salt-/tidal-marsh studies, 26 transferable coastal-wetland studies, and 65 review, contextual and methodological sources. The synthesis shows that optical, hyperspectral, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), LiDAR and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) data are most defensible when treated as complementary sources of spectral, structural and hydrological evidence rather than as direct measurements of total carbon stock. Recent site-specific studies illustrate high performance under particular calibration conditions, but their metrics are not pooled because targets, validation designs, spatial resolutions and study settings differ substantially. Field biomass plots, sediment cores, bulk density, organic carbon, vertical-datum control and independent validation therefore remain essential for accounting-grade blue-carbon estimates. The review further identifies feature-level fusion as a practical default for interpretable multi-sensor modeling, while highlighting the spatial-resolution limits of open Sentinel baselines for narrow and fragmented marshes. Finally, we distinguish demonstrated wetland/coastal digital-twin components from an original salt-marsh digital-twin research agenda proposed here. The agenda links observation-driven state updating, eco-geomorphic models, scenario testing, uncertainty and adaptive management without implying that operational salt-marsh digital twins are already established. Priority needs are stronger tropical and subtropical evidence, reproducible evidence inventories, transferability tests, uncertainty-aware validation and practitioner-ready monitoring workflows. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: Partially automated truck fleets, consisting of both Automated Trucks (ATs) and Human-Driven Trucks (HDTs), are expected to be the operational norm in Automated Container Terminals (ACTs) for the foreseeable future. Right-of-Way (ROW) allocation has emerged as an effective approach for coordinating such heterogeneous fleets. However, existing ROW methods struggle to handle HDT-induced disruptions due to insufficient consideration of HDT behavioral uncertainties. To address this gap, this paper proposes a robust ROW allocation method tailored for mixed-traffic ACTs. The proposed method features: i) reduces conflicts involving uncertainties in turning intentions of HDTs; ii) addresses impedance caused by slow-moving HDTs; iii) achieves high computational efficiency while maintaining high solution quality. Methodologically, the proposed method is formulated as a three-stage stochastic optimization framework. First, an inference engine predicts the probabilities of HDT turning maneuvers. Second, a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model is constructed to optimize passage timing, sequencing, and overtaking decisions across high-probability turning scenarios. To meet real-time computational demands, a customized Benders Branch-and-Cut (BB&C) algorithm is developed, enhanced with several acceleration strategies, including the generation of strong optimality cuts. Finally, a robustness criterion based on expected net benefit is employed to select the optimal allocation scheme under turning uncertainty. Simulation experiments based on a high-fidelity digital twin of a real-world terminal are conducted. Results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in conflict resolution, impedance mitigation, and terminal operational efficiency. Additionally, the operational feasibility domain regarding fleet size and HDT ratio is identified. Furthermore, the algorithm achieves millisecond-level computation times, confirming its feasibility for real-time deployment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Sediment–groundwater interfaces regulate the mobilisation, transport, and attenuation of metal contaminants within highly heterogeneous and multi-scale subsurface systems. However, efforts to operationalise digital twins in this domain remain fragmented across modelling paradigms, disciplines, and scales of observation and prediction. This study provides a performance-centred, quantitatively harmonised meta-analysis of sediment–groundwater digital twin (SG-DT) implementations, explicitly addressing scale dependence, spatial heterogeneity, and process-level controls. A PRISMA 2020–compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of 175 studies (1997–2026; 27 countries) was conducted. SG-DT applications were stratified across a continuum from pore and laboratory scales to site, reach, and basin domains. Scaling effects were analysed via stratified synthesis and meta-regression, while heterogeneity was operationalised through facies-based zonation, parameter variability, and multi-source observational constraints. Predictive performance was quantified using a redesigned, baseline-consistent effect size (E), enabling harmonisation across heterogeneous metrics and validation protocols. Uncertainty was estimated using random-effects models (REML) with Hartung–Knapp adjustments, and heterogeneity was assessed via τ2 and I2 with scale-aware interpretation. Results indicate a robust positive pooled performance gain for surrogate-enabled SG-DTs relative to non-updating baselines under scale-consistent validation, while highlighting limitations related to data dependence and extrapolation. In a subset of comparable studies, SG-DTs achieved a pooled out-of-sample R2 of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.62–0.72). Meta-regression identifies continuous data assimilation and explicit uncertainty quantification as key drivers of performance, whereas residual heterogeneity reflects unresolved scale mismatches and inconsistent representation of subsurface complexity. SG-DTs are defined as systems coupling a process-informed hydro(geo)chemical core capturing reaction kinetics and flow–transport–geochemical coupling, streaming observations, and an updating operator within a closed-loop framework. As secondary outputs, we provide a scale-aware reference architecture embedded in a continuous verification–validation–uncertainty quantification loop and the SED-GW-DT-REPORT v1.0 standard for reproducible, FAIR-aligned reporting. These findings establish an auditable, scale-consistent evidence base for advancing reliable digital twin development in sediment–groundwater systems. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Cyber-Resilient Digital Twin Architectures for Smart Grids: A Review of Attack Modeling, Detection, Mitigation, and Secure Control Strategies

Authors with affiliations: Ogiesoba-Eguakun O.C., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States; Rath S., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States
Abstract: The digitalization of smart grids has expanded the cyberattack surface of critical energy infrastructure, creating a need for security mechanisms that integrate communication behavior, physical-system dynamics, and resilient control. Digital twins provide a promising foundation for this integration, but existing research remains fragmented across system architectures, threat models, defense methods, and validation environments. The aim of this review is to identify, classify, and critically compare how cyber-resilient DT architectures support the smart-grid cybersecurity lifecycle across DT architecture, cyber–physical attack modeling, detection and mitigation, secure control and recovery, and experimental validation. A structured multi-database search of Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library identified 1627 records. After duplicate removal, publication-type exclusions, and eligibility assessment, 149 publications were retained for thematic synthesis and quality appraisal. The evidence indicates that a qualifying cyber-resilient digital twin is distinguished not merely by the presence of a virtual model, but by bidirectional physical–virtual synchronization combined with explicit cyber-resilience functions. Cyberattack studies span measurement, communication, control, device and infrastructure, and coordinated attack surfaces, although study-specific assumptions regarding attacker access and compromised interfaces frequently limit direct comparison. Physics-based detectors offer strong interpretability and real-time suitability but remain sensitive to model and topology errors, whereas data-driven methods capture complex attack patterns but depend on representative data and may generalize poorly. Federated learning preserves data locality but introduces privacy, poisoning, and communication concerns, while moving target defense and deception provide complementary proactive capabilities. No detection or mitigation strategy is uniformly superior across attack coverage, interpretability, false-alarm behavior, latency, scalability, and computational burden. DT-enabled secure control and self-healing further require safety-constrained mitigation under detection uncertainty, communication delay, model mismatch, and partially compromised information. Validation is dominated by simulation, with comparatively little hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) or utility-scale field evidence. Key research gaps include inconsistent digital twin terminology, limited benchmark datasets, synchronization and model-fidelity challenges, inadequate interoperability, and insufficient validation of autonomous mitigation. This review contributes an integrated taxonomy and decision-oriented framework for evaluating and selecting cyber-resilient digital twin strategies for smart grids. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Flexible operation subjects coal-fired utility boilers to distinct but interacting combustion, emissions and equipment-safety constraints at low load and during rapid load changes. This review synthesises 203 publications on sensing, prediction, dynamic modelling, optimisation and system integration, linking operating problems to measurements, model resolution and validation requirements. Low-load operating points are better documented than plant responses during ramps. Low-load assessment centres on ignition, burnout and heating-surface conditions; ramping also requires attention to fuel delivery, steam/water dynamics and selective catalytic reduction. Low-order dynamic models support load-tracking analysis, whereas spatially resolved or coupled models address local heat transfer and tube-wall constraints. Validation must distinguish steady regression, transient forecasting and control, and test transfer across relevant fuels and operating conditions. Predicted optimisation gains require independent evaluation before they support claims of plant benefit. For plant application, selected settings must be linked to operating constraints and measured responses, with benefit attribution accounting for fuel and load differences and uncertainty. System integration, physical implementation and repeated automatic feedback remain distinct. Future work should combine complementary measurements with task-appropriate models and independently evaluate the resulting operating actions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: The increasing penetration of variable solar and wind generation requires flexible resources capable of improving energy balancing, reliability, and renewable energy utilization. This review critically assesses biofuel-integrated hybrid energy systems as complementary architectures for renewable energy integration, connecting system configuration, energy conversion efficiency, storage and dispatch, intelligent control, environmental performance, and scalability. A critical narrative and integrative approach was applied using literature retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, and organized across solar–bioenergy, wind–bioenergy, multi-source, storage-supported, microgrid, and multi-energy configurations. The evidence indicates that biomass-derived fuels can provide dispatchable and storable renewable energy that complements variable generation and supports decentralized and multi-energy applications. However, no architecture is universally superior, and greater hybridization does not inherently result in higher thermodynamic efficiency. Performance depends strongly on resource complementarity, feedstock availability and quality, conversion pathways, storage requirements, and operating strategy. Advanced energy management, model predictive control, machine learning, and digital twins can improve system coordination, although much of the available evidence remains simulation-based or limited in experimental scale. Environmental benefits are likewise pathway- and boundary-dependent, particularly when avoided emissions, coproduct allocation, infrastructure, and feedstock supply chains are considered. Overall, biofuel-integrated hybrid systems represent an application-dependent flexibility option rather than a universally optimal solution; future progress requires dynamic uncertainty-aware modeling, harmonized techno-economic and life-cycle assessment, and greater pilot- and industrial-scale validation. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Artificial Intelligence for Lithium-Ion Batteries: Closed-Loop Discovery, State Prediction, and Trustworthy Management
Affiliations: School of Resources and Environment, Chengdu University of Information Technology, Chengdu, 610225, China; Institute of Nuclear and New Energy Technology, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming lithium-ion battery (LIB) research by linking heterogeneous data, predictive modeling, mechanistic interpretation, and experimental validation within a closed-loop paradigm. AI does not uniquely enable nonlinear representation; rather, it complements electrochemical, statistical, and control models by learning high-dimensional relationships among composition, structure, processing, interfacial chemistry, operating history, and performance. This review critically examines three connected domains: AI-assisted materials discovery, battery state prediction, and trustworthy intelligent management. To distinguish this contribution from recent topic-specific surveys, we organize methods along four complementary axes—model architecture, learning strategy, physics integration, and deployment strategy—and compare landmark studies using quantitative evidence such as independent cell count, validation design, reported error, experimental budget, and closed-loop acceleration. Materials applications include cathodes, anodes, liquid and solid electrolytes, and electrode-electrolyte interphases; operational applications include state of charge, state of health, remaining useful life, degradation diagnosis, safety warning, and digital twin-enabled management. The critical synthesis identifies data leakage, inconsistent metadata, domain shift, uncalibrated uncertainty, black-box reasoning, computational constraints, and limited external validation as recurring barriers. Future progress will depend less on model complexity alone than on FAIR data, cell-independent evaluation, physics-informed learning, uncertainty-aware decisions, autonomous experimentation, human oversight, and deployment-aware design. These elements define an evidence chain for moving LIB AI from proof-of-concept prediction toward reproducible, closed-loop, and trustworthy battery innovation. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Introduces programmable essential oil delivery architectures for adaptive food systems

Abstract: Background: Essential oils (EOs) have emerged as promising natural alternatives to synthetic food preservatives owing to their broad-spectrum antimicrobial, antioxidant, antifungal, and antibiofilm activities. However, their practical application in food systems remains limited by high volatility, oxidative instability, hydrophobicity, uncontrolled release behavior, and inconsistent performance within complex food matrices. Scope and approach: This review introduced a reprogramming paradigm for EO valorization through the integration of programmable delivery architectures, process intensification (PI), artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, and multi-omics technologies. Unlike previous reviews that primarily address extraction, antimicrobial activity, or encapsulation independently, this work adopts a systems-level perspective that links molecular mechanisms, advanced materials, intensified processing, computational intelligence, and translational implementation within a unified framework for adaptive food preservation. Key findings and conclusions: Recent advances in nanostructured and stimuli-responsive delivery systems, including nanoemulsions, nanostructured lipid carriers, electrospun nanofibers, mesoporous nanomaterials, and biohybrid carriers, have enhanced EO stability, encapsulation efficiency, and controlled-release performance. PI technologies offer opportunities to improve extraction efficiency, sustainability, and manufacturing scalability, whereas AI, machine learning, IoT-enabled sensing, image-based food quality assessment, digital twins, and multi-omics analytics provide powerful tools for predictive optimization, real-time monitoring, and mechanistic elucidation of EO–food–microbe interactions. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist, including limited scalability, food matrix complexity, sensory constraints, fragmented datasets, poor interoperability, regulatory uncertainty, and insufficient industrial validation. This review identifies interconnected scientific, engineering, and digital bottlenecks and proposes a comprehensive gap–solution framework and strategic research roadmap. A conceptual foundation for intelligent, closed-loop EO preservation systems capable of adaptive and predictive functionality is presented. Collectively, this review advances EO research beyond conventional preservation approaches toward scalable, sustainable, and digitally integrated food preservation systems aligned with next-generation industrial and circular bioeconomy objectives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A Digital Twin and Probabilistic Optimization Framework for Resistance Spot-Welded Joints in Automotive Applications
Source title: Journal of Research and Applications in Mechanical Engineering
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, SKN Sinhgad College of Engineering, Maharashtra, 413304, India; Department of Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Karmayogi Institute of Technology, Maharashtra, 413304, India
Authors with affiliations: Kulkarni P.P., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, SKN Sinhgad College of Engineering, Maharashtra, 413304, India; Kulkarni P.R., Department of Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Karmayogi Institute of Technology, Maharashtra, 413304, India
Abstract: This study formulates a digital twin–driven probabilistic model to forecast and optimize the tensile behavior of resistance spot-welded (RSW) galvanized steel auto-body joints. Experimental experimentation was performed on multi-spot cross-tension specimens by a Taguchi L27 design with the considerations of welding current (8959–9554 A), sheet thickness (0.19–0.30 mm), electrode force (350–497 N), weld spot number (2–8), and radial distance (12–16 mm). Tensile strength varied from 4.08 Kgf to 150.91 Kgf. A linear regression model accomplished ±5% prediction accuracy in this range, with thickness and number of welds as the most significant parameters, and radial distance as having a significantly negative effect on strength. To offset the weakness of regression, finite element analysis (FEA) was systematically incorporated, allowing for a mechanistic understanding of stress concentrations due to off-center weld placement and to confirm the observed empirical trends. The FEA also showed predictive validity, with calculations at an unseen parameter set (9554 A, 0.27 mm, 350 N, 8 spots) approximating tensile strength to 145.2 Kgf versus the tested 150.9 Kgf (3.7% error). Parameter uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo simulations with Latin Hypercube Sampling (170 runs), and Global Sensitivity Analysis indicated sheet thickness and weld radius as overall factors on strength variability. Dynamic tensile testing (1.32–2.00 m/min) validated the model's insensitivity to service-relevant strain rates. Together, the synergy from the combination of regression, FEA, and probabilistic simulations provides a predictive digital twin approach that is both statistically sound and mechanistically interpretable. The approach improves weld performance assessment reliability and provides scalable applicability towards lightweight and safe automotive structures. © 2026, Thai Society of Mechanical Engineers (TSME). Abstract: Civil infrastructure assets are managed today through inspection cycles and calendar-based interventions that observe an asset only at discrete instants, so deterioration between visits is inferred rather than measured. Digital Twin (DT) research has addressed parts of this problem, but published frameworks remain confined either to a single lifecycle phase or to a single enabling technology, and few report reproducible validation against public benchmarks. This paper presents a unified DT framework that couples a cyber-physical sensing and communication layer, an entropy-weighted multi-sensor fusion scheme, a hybrid physics-plus-machine-learning surrogate, extended Kalman assimilation for continuous model updating, and a constrained multi-objective optimisation layer that closes the loop from measurement to intervention across all five lifecycle phases of an asset. The contribution is threefold: a phase-invariant state formulation in which design, construction, operation, maintenance and end-of-life are expressed as a single evolving state trajectory; an adaptive physics-to-data blending coefficient calibrated on held-out data rather than fixed a priori; and a reliability-constrained decision layer in which maintenance actions are selected subject to an explicit failure-probability bound. The framework is exercised on a provisional synthetic dataset generated deterministically from a calibrated finite element model of a three-span reinforced concrete girder bridge, and is benchmarked against traditional, IoT-only and AI-only baselines under an identical protocol. All reported results are simulation outcomes; no field validation, laboratory validation or real-time deployment has been performed. The DT configuration attains 96.0% detection accuracy, with a 95% Wilson interval of 95.0 to 96.8, and an area under the curve of 0.98, against 90.0% and 0.92 for the strongest AI-only baseline, every pairwise difference being significant at p below 0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment. Remaining useful life error falls from 4.80 to 1.30 years, median end-to-end latency from 250 ms to 120 ms, and the annual failure rate from 0.080 to 0.020, raising twenty-year reliability from 0.202 to 0.670 with a discounted break-even at year 5.8. Detection accuracy remains at or above 92% across high-temperature, heavy-load and seismic operating states. A component ablation attributes the margin principally to environmental normalisation at 7.4 percentage points, the physics constraint at 6.0 and continuous assimilation at 4.8, rather than to model capacity, which is held constant against the AI-only baseline. Deployment barriers - interoperability, cybersecurity, cost, power and validation under uncertainty - are quantified and mapped to mitigation measures and residual risk, and a reproducibility statement specifies the dataset generator, splits, hyperparameters, seeds and computing environment, from which every reported figure is exactly reproducible. © 2026 Seventh Sense Research Group®.

Title: Blockchain-driven authenticated cryptography-based Canetti–Krawczyk security leakage policy for energy transition in e-shared mobility transportation and charging station with applied renewable diversified utilization and social-travel welfare in sustainable cities

Abstract: Urban energy systems need coordinated operation of low-carbon energy resources and mobility services under renewable uncertainty, market variability, and cyber-physical constraints. This paper develops an uncertainty-aware scheduling framework for a virtual multi-carrier energy system coupled with hybrid electric compressed natural gas passenger-car mobility. The quantitatively modeled core of the framework includes multi-carrier dispatch, reserve allocation, renewable curtailment control, and risk-aware scheduling under stochastic uncertainty. Chance-constrained programming and scenario-based uncertainty modeling are used to represent variations in renewable generation, loads, energy prices, and vehicle mobility behavior. CVaR-based risk preferences are incorporated to compare conservative and risk-taking operating strategies within a hierarchical decision structure. The computational implementation evaluates the proposed model on benchmark and large-scale urban energy-mobility systems involving electricity, heat, gas, hydrogen, and transportation layers. The cyber-physical components, including blockchain-based coordination, Canetti-Krawczyk authentication logic, digital-twin synchronization, and IoT-edge-fog-cloud communication, are used as a supervisory architecture for secure data exchange, settlement traceability, and control-signal validation rather than as independently benchmarked security protocols. Numerical results show that the expected operating cost decreases by 69 % when the system shifts from fully conservative operation to a risk-taking strategy, while feasibility is maintained across the coupled energy and mobility subsystems. Power-to-gas integration also reduces emission intensity from 981.30 g/kWh to 362.47 g/kWh under risk-averse operation and from 723.27 g/kWh to 413.87 g/kWh under risk-taking operation, corresponding to reductions of 63.1 % and 42.9 %, respectively. The results indicate that coordinated multi-carrier scheduling and HE-CNG mobility flexibility can reduce cost and emission intensity while preserving risk-controlled operation and network feasibility. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: This paper develops a digital-twin workflow for batch chocolate conching by integrating a hybrid grey-box dynamic model with the Bees Algorithm (BA) to synthesize constraint-satisfying operating policies and additive schedules. The modelling contribution is a compact, equation-driven representation that couples (i) event-driven phase progression (dry–plastic–liquid), (ii) temperature–mixing–aeration accelerated moisture and volatile stripping, and (iii) structure-governed Herschel–Bulkley rheology via an interpretable closure linking a latent coating/dispersion index to yield stress and consistency evolution. The optimization contribution is a band-constrained formulation that enforces industrial rheology bands together with strict limits on residual moisture/volatiles and caps on maximum temperature and specific energy, while enabling early-stop termination once feasibility is sustained over a discharge-relevant hold window. Industrial-scale experiments were conducted on an instrumented 2.5-t conche at MEMAK using three batches, with two batches used for parameter calibration and one batch retained for independent cross-validation. Measured temperature and power/energy trajectories, together with discrete rheology, moisture, and volatile-marker measurements, were used to estimate uncertain model parameters and to provide a preliminary assessment of predictive performance under the investigated formulation and operating conditions. Simulation–experiment agreement was quantified using trajectory-level error metrics and discharge-relevant hold-window comparisons. The optimized policy achieved ηref = 3.229 Pa·s within the prescribed 3–5 Pa·s range and τy = 7.165 Pa within the 7–9 Pa range, while satisfying moisture, volatile, temperature, and specific-energy constraints and enabling early termination at 451.7 min. Given the limited three-batch dataset, these results should be interpreted as preliminary industrial-scale calibration and cross-validation rather than definitive evidence of plant-wide robustness. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: Multiscale damage modeling of fiber reinforced composites (FRCs) is a central scientific issue for ensuring their service reliability in critical engineering fields such as aerospace and advanced equipment. This review systematically reviews recent advances in multiscale modeling techniques for FRCs damage simulation, with the aim of clarifying the underlying logic, coupling mechanisms, and development trends of different modeling strategies, thereby providing a theoretical support for next generation high fidelity predictive systems. This work firstly elaborates the fundamental theories of multiscale modeling, summarizes the evolution paths of cross-scale damage and classical failure criteria, and clarifies the carrier function of representative volume element (RVE) in cross-scale information transmission. Subsequently, a critical evaluation is conducted on various mainstream modeling strategies to reveal their essential distinctions and complementary scopes between mechanism-oriented and efficiency-oriented paradigms. Furthermore, hierarchical validation strategies for multiscale modeling are discussed. Combined with sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification techniques, an evaluation framework ranging from single-scale self-consistency to full-scale closed-loop assessment is established. Finally, current research challenges are analyzed, and four major frontier directions are identified: dynamic mapping between manufacturing defects and service performance, construction of multiscale multiphysics coupled models, deep integration of physics and data-driven modeling, and closed loop evolution of digital twins. This review is intended to provide a systematic and forward looking perspective for future research in this field and to promote the development of multiscale damage models for FRCs with higher computational efficiency and stronger predictive capability. © 2026

Abstract: Forest Land Use Intensity (F-LUI) is a multidimensional and dynamic property of forest ecosystems that cannot be directly observed by Remote Sensing (RS). Existing approaches commonly quantify individual management activities, forest attributes or ecological responses and therefore capture only specific dimensions of forest-use intensity. This concept-driven narrative review proposes a trait-based conceptual framework in which forest traits constitute the common observational interface linking anthropogenic forest use, ecosystem responses and RS observations. Based on this principle forest traits and their spatial, temporal and functional expressions are interpreted within six complementary F-LUI indicator families: Trait, Genesis, Structure, Taxonomy, Function and Socio-economics. Rather than defining a universal F-LUI index, the framework provides a multidimensional, sensor-independent architecture for integrating RS with in situ observations, forest inventories, management information and environmental data. Emerging approaches including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Foundation Models, multi-sensor data fusion, semantic technologies, Knowledge Graphs and Digital Twins may support its operationalisation. Key challenges remain in standardisation, uncertainty quantification, attribution of management effects and transferability across forest types, management regimes and spatial and temporal scales. The proposed framework provides an open and extensible basis for harmonised, reproducible and operational trait-based monitoring of F-LUI. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: From smart sensing to adaptive remediation: artificial intelligence and Internet of Things for persistent organic pollutants

Abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) remain a major environmental challenge because of their persistence, long-range transport, bioaccumulation, and resistance to degradation. Conventional monitoring and remediation systems provide reliable analytical performance but are largely fragmented, laboratory dependent, and unable to deliver the continuous, predictive, and adaptive management required for complex, dynamic contamination scenarios. Recent literature reports substantial advances in biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) for pollutant detection, forecasting, source identification, and remediation optimization. However, these developments often operate separately, with limited coordination between environmental sensing, data analytics, treatment processes, and decision-making. The literature further highlights persistent barriers to field deployment, including limited and geographically heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent sensor performance and calibration, restricted model transferability, insufficient independent validation, uncertainty in AI predictions, and the lack of mature regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted environmental assessment. From our perspective, the next advance in POP management should move beyond isolated AI applications toward integrated, closed-loop AI–IoT architectures that continuously connect sensing, prediction, remediation, and feedback control. Such systems could transform POP management from reactive assessment to proactive and adaptive environmental governance. Future progress will depend on standardized, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) environmental datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, robust field validation, and interoperable sensing infrastructures. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: A multiscale modeling roadmap for interphases in fiber-reinforced thermoplastics: linking molecular mechanisms, mesoscale morphology, and structural response

Abstract: Although poised to be key strategic materials for achieving lightweight and recyclable solutions, the full potential of fiber reinforced thermoplastics hinges on advanced fiber-matrix interphase research. Yet, multiscale simulations linking molecular architectures to macroscale responses remain critically fragmented. We addresses this gap by systematically deconstructing the fundamental interphase physics, spanning thermodynamic wetting, reptation-mediated interdiffusion, confined heterogeneous crystallization, and hygrothermal degradation. Next, we elucidate the bottom-up assembly of chemically specific interphases via atomistic and coarse-grained modeling, leveraging resolution-bridging protocols to derive robust interfacial constitutive laws. Integrating these with mesoscale frameworks captures morphological heterogeneity, establishing a predictive link to macroscopic composite performance. Crucially, bridging fundamental interfacial science and structural engineering, we detail how process-dependent interphase properties dictate hybrid failure modes and architecture-mediated responses. This underscores the imperative of an Integrated Computational Materials Engineering framework for processing-aware structural design. To overcome data scarcity and ill-posed scale-bridging problems, we highlight Physics-Guided Machine Learning and inverse strategies. Coupling Bayesian uncertainty quantification with scalable data infrastructures accelerates interphase-centered design. Ultimately, we outline a comprehensive roadmap fusing physics-based and data-driven paradigms to realize closed-loop, processing-aware digital twins for next-generation FRTPs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Lesme G.L.E.
Title: Digital twins in medicine: between simulating the future and clinical uncertainty.; [Gemelos digitales en medicina: entre la simulación del futuro y la incertidumbre clínica.]
Source title: Revista de la Federacion Argentina de Cardiologia
Affiliations: Hospital Nacional de Itagua, Paraguay
Authors with affiliations: Lesme G.L.E., Hospital Nacional de Itagua, Paraguay
Abstract: It is an undeniable fact that science has evolved extraordinarily. Each discovery and new tool has served as a foundation for the next, enabling us to better understand the world and solve problems that until recently seemed impossible. Yet, it faces a paradox today: never before has so much information about patients been available, and at the same time, never has it been so difficult to integrate that information into a truly coherent representation of their biology. The next step for artificial intelligence seems almost natural: constructing an individualized, dynamic, and predictive virtual representation of a patient, organ, or biological system; in other words, a digital twin. More than just a computer copy, it aims to be a model updated with data from its real-world counterpart, capable of simulating trajectories and exploring responses to various interventions. In cardiology, this concept has already driven the development of models for phenotyping, prediction, electrophysiology, and therapeutic selection. © 2026, Federacion Argentina de Cardiologia. Authors: Li X.; Gao Y.; Shi L.
Title: Exercise adaptation and proactive health: an information-theoretic framework based on load entropy
Affiliations: China Institute of Sport Science, General Administration of Sport of China, Beijing, China; Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University, Zhuhai, China; Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Authors with affiliations: Li X., China Institute of Sport Science, General Administration of Sport of China, Beijing, China, Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University, Zhuhai, China; Gao Y., Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Shi L., Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University, Zhuhai, China
Abstract: Exercise is among the most powerful stimuli for promoting health, yet exercise science still prescribes load largely through fixed, population-derived intensity zones that overlook how individuals perceive and adapt to training stimuli. This review develops Proactive Health as a scientific framework in which exercise is the central means of cultivating adaptive capacity and introduces an information-theoretic model - load entropy - to explain why individuals respond differently to the same exercise challenge. Drawing on principles from complexity science, information theory and non-equilibrium thermodynamics, the framework conceptualises health as adaptive capacity rather than the absence of disease and positions entropy as a central organising principle of biological adaptation. Within this view, health is reframed as adaptive capacity rather than the absence of disease, and entropy becomes a central organising principle of biological adaptation: exercise perturbs the system, transiently raises local entropy and informational uncertainty, and thereby triggers the self-organised reorganisation that underlies training adaptation. Building on psychophysics, the load entropy model reconceptualises exercise load not as a purely mechanical scalar but as the perceptual uncertainty an individual experiences in discriminating a stimulus, which peaks at an entropy-defined "effective stimulus"- a hypothesised, individually and momentarily specific threshold of maximal adaptive challenge. We show how this construct connects to established practice such as heart-rate-variability-guided training and load monitoring, and how it could inform personalised exercise prescription, rehabilitation and digital-twin, AI-enabled care. As a conceptual and hypothesis-driven review, the work generates testable hypotheses for personalised exercise prescription, rehabilitation and exercise monitoring and provides a translational framework for proactive, adaptive healthcare. © 2026 the author(s), published by De Gruyter on behalf of Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Guangzhou Sport University.

Title: A physics-informed simulation-based digital twin framework for condition monitoring and health assessment of automotive suspension systems
Affiliations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, 632014, India
Authors with affiliations: Rajamohan V., School of Mechanical Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, 632014, India
Abstract: In the present study, a physics-informed simulation-based digital twin framework for an automotive suspension system exposed to transient and stochastic road excitations is formulated for health monitoring and prognostics. A physics-based quarter-car dynamic model is considered for the development of governing equation of motion and integrated with the state estimation and online damping parameter tracking to synchronize the virtual model with the simulated degrading physical system. Further, the proposed framework is assessed through obtaining the response data under controlled road excitations, where the prescribed road displacement and velocity serve as excitation inputs during the state estimation process. A normalized suspension health index (SHI) is obtained continuously from the estimated damping coefficient to quantify its degradation in real time. Initially, remaining useful life (RUL) of the suspension system is evaluated using the conventional slope-based degradation approach. The numerical instability of the slope-based approach is evident from the presence of artificial spikes and projection of unreliable life. However, this limitation is overcome through developing a cumulative damage-based prognostic of suspension system such that the life degradation is expressed in terms of integral of degradation of intensity of the damping coefficient, obtained through SHI. The comparative analysis under half-cosine bump and stochastic road inputs demonstrates that the proposed damage-based RUL approach provides stable, interpretable, and monotonic prognostic estimates. Further, the robustness of the proposed framework against the various uncertainties in vehicle loading is investigated through performing a mass sensitivity analysis. The various uncertainties such as the variation in the sprung mass depending on passenger occupancy, payload, and operating conditions are considered for the investigation. Further, the results demonstrate that the proposed digital twin framework enhances the robustness and reliability of suspension life prediction through integrating the time-varying damping coefficient, SHI, and cumulative damage modelling. It can be concluded that the proposed simulation-based digital twin framework yields a scalable foundation for the physics-informed health monitoring, prognostic studies and offers a extensible basis for future real-world implementation. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Physics-data fusion-based dynamic model updating of semi-direct-drive offshore wind turbine gearboxes using full-scale test data

Abstract: Accurate dynamic modeling of offshore wind turbine gearboxes is essential for vibration response prediction, condition monitoring, and reliability-oriented operation of wind turbine drivetrains under complex offshore conditions. However, conventional models based on nominal parameters often fail to match measured responses because of uncertainties in mesh stiffness, support properties, damping and transmission errors. This study proposes a physics-data fusion-based dynamic model updating framework for semi-direct-drive offshore wind turbine planetary gearboxes using full-scale test data. A coupled gear-bearing dynamic model is established by incorporating time-varying mesh stiffness, nonlinear support forces, damping, and comprehensive transmission error. The uncertain dynamic parameters are normalized and evaluated through dependent sensitivity analysis to identify the dominant contributors to vibration-response discrepancies. These parameters are subsequently updated using a physically constrained optimization strategy driven by measured vibration data. The proposed framework is calibrated and validated using vibration measurements from a full-scale wind turbine gearbox test platform. Results show that the updated model significantly improves the agreement between simulated and measured vibration responses and more accurately captures the dynamic characteristics of the planetary gear train. The proposed approach provides a practical basis for high-fidelity drivetrain modeling and supports condition assessment, maintenance optimization, and digital-twin-enabled reliability management for offshore wind turbines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Hydrogen storage remains a central bottleneck for scalable hydrogen energy systems due to the multiscale and coupled nature of the thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural evolution of hydrogen storage materials (HSMs). Although artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated materials discovery, current approaches remain constrained by fragmented data, limited physical consistency, and weak integration with experimental validation. Here, we propose a unified framework that integrates coherent data infrastructure, physics-grounded modeling, and AI-driven inverse design within a closed-loop discovery paradigm. By constraining optimization with thermodynamics, kinetics, uncertainty, provenance, and experimental feedback, this approach enables adaptive, physically consistent optimization, thereby establishing a pathway toward autonomous, digital-twin-enabled discovery of HSMs. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Integrating global crop models with knowledge graphs: Evolution, comparison, and future directions

Abstract: Crop models leverage mathematical methods to simulate plant growth and environmental responses, forming a powerful and critical tool for agricultural decision support in research, management, and policy–making. However, a comprehensive review that systematically integrates global crop model resources with knowledge graphs linking their evolution to applications remains absent. Here, following a review of mainstream crop models, we constructed a multidimensional comparison framework to offer a more comprehensive overview, covering application areas, structural features, functional modules, and applicable crop types. We systematically integrated mainstream international crop models databases by classified key crop models into three groups based on their primary drivers and system scales. Mechanistic crop models focus on internal photosynthetic physiology. Process–based crop models simulate the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum, emphasizing resource movement and water–use efficiency. Integrated system crop models operate at the ecosystem level, addressing long–term dynamics like crop rotation, soil biogeochemistry, and management impacts. Subsequently, we performed a bibliometric analysis of relevant literature from 2013 to 2024 using CiteSpace. This analysis identified three primary research hotspots for crop models, i.e. enhancing yield simulation capabilities, assessing climate change impacts, and developing decision support systems for production management. Finally, we identified key limitations and prospective trends. The fundamental constraints are: (1) the disruption of model–reliant steady–state climate parameters by extreme weather; (2) the challenges of cultivar parameterization and local calibration; and (3) insufficient mechanistic understanding of pest/disease/weed dynamics, along with uncertainties in coupling model modules. Despite these challenges, we identify three development directions that are each supported by both the model comparison and the bibliometric analysis: remote-sensing data assimilation, integration with machine learning, and cross-cutting directions covering digital twins and multi-model coupling. Abstract: Tunnel leakage threatens the durability, safety, and serviceability of underground infrastructure, while conventional inspection methods remain limited by low efficiency, subjectivity, and poor capability for hidden seepage assessment. This review aims to clarify recent progress in artificial intelligence-based tunnel leakage detection and monitoring by examining sensing technologies, intelligent interpretation methods, and multimodal fusion strategies from a measurement-oriented perspective. Electromagnetic, optical, mechanical, vibration/acoustic, environmental, wireless, self-powered, and multi-parameter sensing approaches are compared according to their measurable quantities, applicable tasks, advantages, limitations, and uncertainty sources. Deep learning methods are discussed in relation to leakage classification, detection, segmentation, localization, quantification, and early warning. The review indicates that vision- and LiDAR-assisted methods are comparatively mature for visible leakage recognition, boundary segmentation, and spatial localization, whereas fiber-optic, acoustic, thermal, and environmental sensing, supported by wireless and self-powered platforms, is better suited to hidden seepage inference, distributed monitoring, and long-term warning. Practical implementation is still constrained by limited annotated datasets, inconsistent calibration, environmental interference, weak cross-tunnel generalization, and insufficient evaluation of measurement robustness. To address these challenges, the Pluralistic Resonant Perception Theory (PRPT) is introduced as a conceptual framework for organizing heterogeneous sensing information, cross-modal interaction, spatiotemporal coordination, and semantic-mechanistic coupling. Future research should emphasize standardized datasets, uncertainty-aware fusion, sensor calibration, edge deployment, digital twins, and field validation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Forest Carbon Sink Estimation under Smart Forestry: Progress, Challenges, and Prospects; [智慧林业背景下森林碳汇估算：进展、挑战与展望]

Abstract: ： Forests constitute the largest carbon reservoir in terrestrial ecosystems, and accurately assessing their carbon sink capacity is essential for maintaining the global carbon balance. However, forest ecosystem carbon sinks exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, making their accurate quantification highly challenging. By integrating multisource information technologies, smart forestry provides new opportunities to overcome the limitations of conventional static monitoring and to support dynamic simulation and precision management. This study systematically reviews the major methods used for forest carbon sink estimation, summarizes their development trends and research hotspots, and provides a comprehensive review of the opportunities and challenges associated with the development of smart forestry. The study results showed that the number of publications on forest carbon sink estimation has increased exponentially worldwide, forming a research landscape centered on China and the United States, with Western Europe and East Asia as major supporting regions. Forest carbon sink estimation has evolved from early reliance on field surveys and empirical statistical methods toward the integrated application of process-based models, remote sensing-driven models, ecosystem service models, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. There are clear differences in research priorities are observed between international and Chinese studies: international research focuses more on climate-response mechanisms at the global scale, while research in China places greater emphasis on high-resolution regional mapping in support of the national carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals. Forest carbon sink assessment has entered a new stage characterized by multi-technology integration and cross-scale coordination. Future research should focus on reducing uncertainties associated with scale transformation and improving model interpretability by applying edge computing to dynamic carbon sink monitoring and risk early warning, strengthening the coupling of ecological process mechanisms with deep learning, and promoting the coordinated use of satellite, airborne, and ground-based observations within digital twin platforms. These advances will help improve the timeliness, accuracy, and decision-support capacity of forest carbon sink estimation. © 2026, Chinese Society of Forestry. All rights reserved.

Title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in multi-energy systems: A review
Affiliations: Department of Energy and Petroleum Engineering, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, 4036, Norway; NORCE Research, Stavanger, 4021, Norway
Authors with affiliations: Vaniar A.M., Department of Energy and Petroleum Engineering, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, 4036, Norway; Karimi A., Department of Energy and Petroleum Engineering, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, 4036, Norway; Beglar K.S., Department of Energy and Petroleum Engineering, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, 4036, Norway; Mansouri M., Department of Energy and Petroleum Engineering, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, 4036, Norway, NORCE Research, Stavanger, 4021, Norway
Abstract: Multi-energy systems (MESs) are becoming harder to operate as decentralization, decarbonization, and digitalization increase uncertainty, coupling, and real-time control pressure. In this setting, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is attractive because it can learn adaptive policies from interaction data without requiring a fully specified plant model. This paper reviews DRL applications across device-level control, grid-level coordination, and higher-level multi-agent and hierarchical decision-making, including market-interaction settings. The synthesis rests on 78 studies retained from 93 articles assessed at full text, identified through a structured search of five bibliographic databases covering literature published from 2018 onwards and screened against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The review traces how the field has moved from single-agent designs toward structured multi-agent and hierarchical formulations to handle hybrid action spaces and heterogeneous assets at scale. It also synthesizes practical trends, including safe RL, transfer learning, federated learning, and digital-twin-based validation. At the device-level, off-policy actor–critic methods (TD3, SAC) dominate continuous control of batteries, HVAC, and CHP units, whereas at the grid-level value-based methods prevail for discrete dispatch and voltage control, where constraint enforcement, rather than reward shaping alone, emerges as the key unresolved requirement. A central conclusion is that reported simulation gains are strong, but deployment readiness still depends on better safety guarantees, sample efficiency, interpretability, and benchmark standardization. Based on these findings, the paper outlines a research agenda aimed at closing the gap between algorithmic performance and dependable real-world MES operation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Digital Twin-Based Resilient Consensus Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Attack
