Abstract: Global-wave hindcast products are widely used as environmental inputs in ship design, weather routing, and maritime digital twins. However, their reliability in regions of strong western boundary currents has not been sufficiently quantified from an engineering perspective. This study investigates the effect of wave–current interaction (WCI) on hindcast accuracy and its propagation into ship responses and propulsion performance. Multi-source validation was conducted using global drifting buoys and full-scale measurements from a very large ore carrier equipped with X-band wave radar and strain gauges operating in the Agulhas Current. While hindcasts show high accuracy in open-ocean conditions, a systematic underestimation of the significant wave height is observed under opposing wave–current alignment. Numerical response analyses demonstrate that this bias propagates into ship engineering assessments: vertical wave bending moments (VWBM) can be underestimated by up to a factor of two. Propulsion simulations further show that current-induced wave amplification could offset the expected power reduction from following currents. These findings highlight the need to incorporate WCI-related uncertainties into operational assessments and provide an uncertainty-based framework for risk-informed maritime applications. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: The accelerating adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) presents new challenges for intelligent, adaptive, and privacy-preserving charge/discharge scheduling. This paper introduces a unified framework that integrates a federated multi-task Transformer with digital twin-enhanced reinforcement learning to perform real-time, uncertainty-aware EV scheduling. The Transformer jointly forecasts key behavioral parameters–arrival time, departure time, and travel mileage–by capturing temporal-spatial dependencies across distributed EV fleets while preserving user privacy through federated learning. A high-fidelity digital twin simulates user behavior, grid conditions, and EV battery dynamics, enabling continual policy adaptation through reinforcement learning. Additionally, conformal prediction is employed to quantify uncertainty and guide decision-making, improving robustness under dynamic and non-stationary environments. Extensive simulations on real-world mobility data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Forecasting accuracy exceeds R2 > 0.99 for arrival time and 0.98 for travel mileage across clusters. In aggregator net revenue optimization, the proposed method delivers up to 15.09% improvement with V2G discharging and over 14% without V2G, outperforming state-of-the-art GAN and TCN baselines. By jointly addressing forecasting, uncertainty quantification, policy learning, and privacy preservation, the proposed framework offers a practical and scalable solution for next-generation EV-grid integration. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: Background: The global food safety crisis and strict traceability demands require integrating complex data obtained using diverse sensors across the supply chain. While artificial intelligence has propelled multi-source fusion, traditional models often struggle to adapt to dynamic real-world environments. To tackle these challenges, biomimetic fusion strategies offer a highly flexible and robust solution. By mimicking biological processes and continuously learning from new information, they effectively integrate complex data obtained from various detection techniques. Scope and approach: Herein, we review recent advances in biomimetic fusion strategies for obtaining multi-source heterogeneous data in food detection. We first categorize sensing data into structured and high-dimensional unstructured data. Guided by the computational intelligence evolution, we analyze the complementary progression, dataset adaptability of three fusion modes: (i) fixed-pattern fusion, which enables efficient and stable integration but has limited flexibility; (ii) dynamic-pattern fusion, which enables context-aware adaptation but incurs greater computational complexity; and (iii) active-pattern fusion, which supports autonomous, goal-directed exploration but faces training instability and environmental dependence. Three mechanisms highlight a synergistic evolution from passive aggregation to intelligent exploration. Finally, by summarizing representative food applications, we highlight future research directions for overcoming key bottlenecks in task-oriented sensor coordination, complex matrix adaptability, resource-efficient active sensing, closed-loop detection, real-world domain shift, and interpretable fusion decision-making. Key findings and conclusions: Biomimetic fusion strategies show immense potential for enhancing food detection accuracy and decision autonomy. By leveraging complementary fixed, dynamic, and active patterns, these strategies drive a paradigm shift from passive aggregation toward active information acquisition. Their applicable boundaries depend primarily on task stability, the need for adaptive representation, and the feasibility of interactive sensing: fixed-pattern fusion is preferred for standardized detection tasks with stable acquisition conditions; dynamic-pattern fusion is more appropriate when fusion relationships must adapt to sample, sensor, or environmental variations; and active-pattern fusion is suitable for open or uncertain scenarios in which the system can iteratively acquire additional information to support decision-making. Across these application boundaries, challenges such as complex food matrices, sensor drift, weak or localized hazards, and limited model interpretability remain. Future advances in uncertainty-driven active sensing, closed-loop feedback, edge computing, digital twins, and lightweight algorithms are expected to support more trustworthy food safety supervision. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Digital Twin-Assisted Chance-Constrained Energy-Aware Scheduling for Self-Sustainable IIoT Networks
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Northern Border University, Arar, 12271, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Alenezi A.H., Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Northern Border University, Arar, 12271, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: On-demand data sensing and Wireless Power Transfer (WPT) enable sustainable operation in large-scale Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) networks. Existing scheduling frameworks are inherently reactive, initiating charging only after an IoT node’s residual energy falls below a predefined threshold, which increases the risk of energy outages and service disruption. This paper proposes a Digital Twin (DT)-enabled proactive scheduling framework for self-sustainable IIoT networks under stochastic operating conditions. The proposed framework integrates three key components. First, a DT layer continuously mirrors IoT node states and predicts future energy availability over a finite prediction horizon. Second, a predictive charging strategy proactively schedules WPT before energy depletion occurs. Third, physical-layer security and DT-based anomaly detection protect the network against eavesdropping, false-data injection, and energy depletion attacks. Fourth, the scheduling framework is reformulated using chance constraints to explicitly account for uncertainty in wireless channels, energy consumption, and DT prediction errors while providing probabilistic reliability guarantees. The resulting sensing and WPT scheduling problems are formulated as multi-slot integer optimization problems and solved using branch-and-bound, with a low-complexity greedy heuristic for latency-sensitive deployments. Simulation results show that the proposed framework reduces energy outage events to below 1%, maintains reliable operation under increasing energy uncertainty with only a modest sensing-utility reduction, and incurs negligible computational overhead compared with the deterministic formulation. © 2026 by the author.

Abstract: Autonomous nanomaterials discovery is rapidly transforming conventional trial-and-error experimentation into intelligent closed-loop scientific ecosystems that integrate artificial intelligence (AI), robotics-assisted experimentation, autonomous characterization, and cyber–physical laboratory infrastructures. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on individual enabling technologies, this critical review presents a systems-level synthesis of autonomous nanomaterials discovery by critically evaluating AI-guided optimization, robotics-assisted synthesis, multimodal characterization, digital twins, foundation models, and sustainability-aware autonomous experimentation within a unified scientific framework. Particular emphasis is placed on the comparative capabilities of machine learning, graph neural networks, generative AI, Bayesian optimization, active learning, and reinforcement learning for adaptive materials discovery, together with their practical limitations in autonomous laboratory environments. Representative applications involving perovskite materials, catalytic nanomaterials, battery materials, and autonomous nanoparticle synthesis illustrate the expanding role of intelligent experimentation platforms in accelerating materials innovation. The review further examines key challenges associated with data quality, uncertainty propagation, interpretability, interoperability, cyber–physical reliability, computational sustainability, and responsible governance that continue to constrain large-scale deployment. Finally, emerging distributed autonomous laboratories, collaborative human–AI scientific workflows, and sustainability-aware multi-objective optimization are identified as key strategic directions for developing trustworthy, resilient, and environmentally responsible autonomous scientific ecosystems. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Digital twin-based energy-efficient framework for smart grid management using RF algorithm

Authors with affiliations: Chen J., Guangdong Shunde Power Design Institute Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, 528300, China; Liang Y., Guangdong Shunde Power Design Institute Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, 528300, China; Lu K., Guangdong Shunde Power Design Institute Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, 528300, China; Wan Z., Guangdong Shunde Power Design Institute Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, 528300, China; Wang X., Guangdong Shunde Power Design Institute Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, 528300, China
Abstract: Modern smart grids face increasing operational uncertainty due to renewable intermittency, dynamic load patterns, and fault-prone distribution networks, which existing reactive control strategies fail to manage effectively. This paper proposes a Digital Twin–based predictive framework to address these challenges. This research suggests a new DT-based framework that will use the Random Forest algorithm as the primary machine learning algorithm for estimating the energy demand, balancing load, and diagnosing faults in power systems. Indeed, by creating favorable and challenging dynamic states, the use of the model increases better decision-making and hence grid stability in addition to complex operational effectiveness. Using these Performance INDEXES, the proposed system is analyzed based on core power system performance metrics including System Average Interruption Duration Index, System Average Interruption Frequency Index and Loss of Load Probability. Linguistic analysis of the results reveals an increase in SAIDI of 15%, SAIFI by 10% and a decrease of the loss of load probability (LOLP) by 8% proving that reliability has been enhanced. Moreover, for overall model of predicting UT grid behavior and managing load, the model accuracy is 93%, which proves validity of the model. MATLAB Simulink is used to simulate the model, which tests how it can be applied in real conditions for dynamic distribution network management along with ensuring its usefulness and applicability for complex, growing networks in the future. © 2026

Title: Digital Twin Engineering with Physics-Informed Neural Networks: State of the Art and Open Challenges
Source title: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used as tools for managing engineering systems through continuous synchronization between physical assets and their virtual counterparts, enabling improved monitoring, prediction and control throughout the system lifecycle. Maintaining accurate alignment requires reliable state estimation from sparse sensor measurements along with adaptive calibration of model parameters to account for degradation, environmental variability and operational uncertainties. Physics informed neural networks address these requirements by embedding governing equations with observational data within a unified optimization framework that supports simultaneous state reconstruction and parameter identification while preserving physical consistency. This review examines the current state of the art in PINN based digital twin synchronization and model updating, presents the mathematical foundations that connect PINNs to classical collocation methods and describes how automatic differentiation enables efficient enforcement of physical constraints. Applications spanning manufacturing, aerospace, energy and infrastructure demonstrate that PINN based digital twins achieve high diagnostic accuracy, low inference latency and significant reductions in operational cost. Key challenges that remain include parameter identifiability, scalability limitations arising from the curse of dimensionality, real time deployment constraints, gaps in validation methodology and robustness to distribution shift. © The Author(s) under exclusive licence to International Center for Numerical Methods in Engineering (CIMNE) 2026.

Title: Reinforcement-Learning-Enabled Supervisory Control of a Full-Scale Anaerobic Digestion Facility Using a Calibrated Digital Twin
Affiliations: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30318, GA, United States; Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter School of Public Policy, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30332, GA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Yunus A.I., School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30318, GA, United States; Jalla S., School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30318, GA, United States; Bozeman J.F., III, School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30318, GA, United States, Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter School of Public Policy, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30332, GA, United States; Chen Y., School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, 30318, GA, United States
Abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a cornerstone of energy recovery and decarbonization at wastewater resource recovery facilities (WRRFs), yet full-scale digesters are often operated conservatively due to delayed process feedback, nonlinear stability constraints, and limited observability. This study presents a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-enabled supervisory control framework for full-scale AD that integrates a calibrated mechanistic digital twin model (DTM) with offline policy learning and counterfactual uncertainty evaluation. Specifically, the DTM was calibrated to reproduce control-relevant digester behavior. Using 2.7 years of simulated operation, a batch-constrained Q (BCQ)-reinforcement learning policy was trained to maximize biogas production while penalizing instability associated with pH excursions and elevated volatile fatty acids (VFAs)/alkalinity (ALK) ratios. Counterfactual evaluation against historical, greedy, and heuristic controls used 1 year unseen DTM simulation and 1 year of full-scale operational data. The RL policy achieved comparable mean daily biogas production (+0.35%) in simulated testing. Under the 1 year operational data, it achieved plant-equivalent mean production of 9802 m3/day, corresponding to a modest potential cumulative improvement (+2.7%, 93 405 m3/year) subject to substantial uncertainty P(Δ > 0) = 0.524. These results indicate that offline-trained RL, combined with a mechanistic digital twin and counterfactual evaluation, provides a feasible and interpretable framework for developing and assessing supervisory AD control without live-plant experimentation while showing that the resulting benefit must be interpreted under explicit model-plant uncertainty. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Controlled user study on the role of situational awareness in design decisions for future lunar In-situ resource utilization systems
Affiliations: Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; European Space Resource Innovation Centre, Luxembourg
Authors with affiliations: Malone L., Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; Cardin M.-A., Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; Cilliers J., Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; Starr S., Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom; Hadler K., Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom, European Space Resource Innovation Centre, Luxembourg
Abstract: As human exploration of the Moon and Mars transitions from temporary missions to long-term habitation, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) is expected to play a pivotal role in enabling future sustainable economic and scientific activities in space. Designing and operating ISRU systems under such extreme and uncertain conditions, however, presents major challenges, ranging from dealing with harsh environmental conditions, regulatory complexity, to differing stakeholder risk tolerance profiles and unpredictable technological system behavior. This study introduces a novel experimental methodology to investigate how human factors playing an important role in situational awareness can influence ISRU-related design decision-making and associated performance under uncertainty. Specifically, this study addresses the following research question: What are the main and interaction effects of different levels of visual fidelity and emotional cues on users’ ability to manage remote lunar resource production systems under uncertainty? A controlled user study involving 33 participants used a serious game platform to explore the effects of two key variables: visual fidelity of the simulation and presence of emotional cues. In a realistic though simplified mission, participants were tasked with operating a simulated lunar ISRU system to supply water sustainably to a lunar habitat. Results show that emotional cues can significantly enhance participants’ performance, measured through a novel operational sustainability metric, particularly in low-fidelity visual environments. The results provide no evidence of statistically significant correlation between situational awareness and system performance. These findings highlight the importance of immersive and affective elements in simulation-based training platforms. The proposed methodology provides a structured, replicable framework to evaluate decision-making in complex space systems, and offers valuable insights into how future ISRU operators, mission architects, and economic actors might be trained more effectively by leveraging immersive technologies like digital twins and virtual reality. Beyond space applications, the approach has potential for broader use in Earth-based industries facing similar operational uncertainties, such as mining in remote conditions and resource production infrastructures. © 2026 The Authors. Abstract: Built-environment assets such as bridges require monitoring methods that support maintenance prioritisation, repair planning, and risk-informed intervention under sparse, noisy data. Physics-informed intelligence, which embeds governing equations, material behaviour, and engineering constraints into deep learning frameworks, has emerged as a promising approach for structurally consistent structural health monitoring and digital twin-enabled bridge asset management. This review synthesises 50 studies published between 2021 and 2026, including 42 primary studies and eight review papers, to provide an evidence-based synthesis of physics-informed intelligence for bridge health monitoring. The synthesis is organised through three components: a taxonomy of architectures, training strategies, applications, and structural types; a seven-criterion quality appraisal with comparison of representative models; and a dependency-gated roadmap for bridge digital twin deployment. This contribution connects method classification, evidence appraisal, and deployment guidance, showing that deployment readiness depends on the engineering prior, validation tier, uncertainty quantification, benchmark comparability, field calibration, and decision-support integration. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Duc N.T.
Title: From mechanistic models to breeding digital twins: Predictive plant improvement for a changing climate
Affiliations: Vietnam National University of Agriculture, Hanoi, Viet Nam
Authors with affiliations: Duc N.T., Vietnam National University of Agriculture, Hanoi, Viet Nam
Abstract: Climate change is making historical phenotypes less reliable guides to future breeding environments, turning prediction into a central problem for plant science. Yet many predictive tools still end at model output, with limited connection to auditable breeding decisions. Here we frame predictive plant improvement as a breeding digital twin problem: a twin must specify a breeding referent, mutable state vector, counterfactual action space, utility function, and prospective audit. Using sweet corn as a stress test, we show how endosperm genetics, product-system quality, seed feasibility, genomic prediction, breeding simulation, and decision science can be organized into auditable breeding intelligence. Rather than replacing fields or breeders, the framework makes crossing, trial, selection, and release decisions more anticipatory under climate uncertainty. The prediction target is not a single phenotype but the joint consequence of breeding decisions for product quality, climate-conditioned resilience, seed feasibility, and program efficiency. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: An Intelligent LLM–Fuzzy Decision Support and Digital Twin Framework for Adaptive Agricultural Robotics Systems
Affiliations: Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Abstract: This study develops an integrated LLM–fuzzy decision-support and digital twin framework for adaptive agricultural robotics, combining semantic reasoning, fuzzy inference, multi-objective optimization, and feedback-driven state updating. Numerical sensor data, operational information, and textual field knowledge are transformed into validated decision rules and model-ready parameters, enabling coordinated decisions across economic, operational, crop-stress, and sustainability-related objectives. The framework is evaluated as a simulation-based proof of concept calibrated with real observations from a semi-smart tomato farm, while controlled digital twin scenarios are used to assess its behavior under environmental and operational disturbances. Compared with numerical optimization alone, the complete LLM–fuzzy framework reduces operational cost by 3.35% and crop stress by 7.98%, while improving operational performance by 4.45%. Ablation, repeated-run, scenario, sensitivity, and dynamic-adaptation analyses further demonstrate consistent computational performance under the evaluated conditions. Sustainability is assessed through a model-based measure integrating water use, energy consumption, and soil-compaction-related impacts. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining semantic reasoning, uncertainty processing, optimization, and digital-twin feedback for adaptive agricultural decision support. However, the results represent a calibrated simulation-based proof of concept rather than validation through a full-scale autonomous field deployment; broader multi-season and field-scale validation is therefore required before generalizing the reported operational and sustainability benefits. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Quantitative pharmacology has guided drug development for decades, turning concentration and response data into mechanistic models that support dosing, trial design, and regulatory decisions. Model-informed drug development (MIDD) did not replace pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling so much as formalize it across the lifecycle. Today, “digital twins” are often promoted as a new paradigm, yet most proposed features mirror established pharmacometrics: individual-level simulation, sequential updating, and decision-focused uncertainty analysis. Title: Orthopedic Mechanophenotype: A Structured Narrative Review of Multiscale Biomechanics, Mechanotransduction, and Clinical Decision-Making
Affiliations: The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; The First People's Hospital of Yunnan Province, Kunming, China
Authors with affiliations: Lan Z., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; Mu Z., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China; Li H., The First School of Clinical Medicine, Yunnan University of Chinese Medicine, Kunming, China, The First People's Hospital of Yunnan Province, Kunming, China
Abstract: Orthopedic disorders are still classified mainly by anatomy or end-stage morphology, yet osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, fracture nonunion, spinal degeneration, and bone-implant interface failure share a common mechanobiological logic: external load is filtered by hierarchical tissue architecture, converted into cell-scale signals, and integrated with inflammation, metabolism, and repair capacity to determine whether adaptation or failure occurs. This structured narrative review synthesizes recent evidence on multiscale biomechanics, finite element analysis (FEA), mechanotransduction biology, tissue engineering, and emerging digital-twin approaches. Rather than introducing a separate disease entity, we define the orthopedic mechanophenotype as a clinically oriented integrative framework that describes the disease-relevant state generated by three interacting axes: load exposure, tissue susceptibility, and biological adaptability. We summarize how this three-axis state differs across bone, articular cartilage and the osteochondral unit, the intervertebral disc, fracture repair, and bone-implant interfaces. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence hierarchy, model assumptions, and persistent uncertainties, including timescale mismatch, idealized boundary conditions, incomplete cross-scale validation, and overinterpretation of cell-level causality from organ-level surrogates. We further illustrate how mechanophenotyping can be integrated with existing clinical pathways for osteoarthritis load redistribution, fracture fixation and rehabilitation, and spinal or implant-related planning. The central argument is that future progress will depend less on accumulating isolated mechanical variables and more on validated cross-scale markers that connect real-world loading, patient-specific structure, and stage-dependent biology to actionable orthopedic decisions. © 2026 The Author(s).
